reason: The second-ranked candidate in the chapter and the one a careful reader is most likely to accept, because the typology is nearly perfect. Genesis 49:28 closes Jacob's deathbed blessing — “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them” — and Mormon 7:1 is the last surviving Nephite's final words to the house of Israel, introduced with “and this is the words which I speak.” A dying patriarch, the house of Israel, and a formula announcing that what follows is his speech. But the verbal contact is the four words “of Israel and this is”, which is an accident of two ordinary clauses abutting, and the two formulas are not the same formula: Genesis 49:28 is a narrator's retrospective summary of a speech already given, Mormon 7:1 is a speaker's own prospective announcement of a speech about to be given. Nothing else of Genesis 49 is present — no tribes, no blessing, no naming. The chapter's real source for its address to the remnant is Isaiah 46:3, linked at this verse, and Isaiah 46:3 happens to open with “O house of Jacob”, which is where the patriarchal resonance actually comes from.

Filed because the anaphora is the most conspicuous formal feature of the chapter and a reader will want to know whether the catalogue tested it. Mormon 7:2-5 open four consecutive verses with “Know ye that ye…”, and “know ye that” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 1 Kings 22:3 (Ramoth in Gilead is ours), Psalm 100:3, Luke 21:31 and Hebrews 13:23 (Timothy is set at liberty). Only Psalm 100:3 is a summons to a people to know a fact about who they and their God are — “Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people” — which is the exact rhetorical situation of Mormon 7:2, “Know ye that ye are of the house of Israel.” The temptation is real and the wording will not bear it: three words, all of them common, and no second point of contact anywhere in the psalm. The Book of Mormon uses “know ye” freely elsewhere without any psalm in view. Recorded so that the register shows the anaphora was examined and declined, not overlooked.

“ye cannot be saved” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 15:1 and Acts 27:31, and both are, like Mormon 7:3, the apodosis of a conditional stating a necessary precondition of salvation: “Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved”; “Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.” Mormon 7:3 has the identical shape — “ye must come unto repentance, or ye cannot be saved.” Rejected on sense, and the sense is not merely different but reversed. Acts 15:1 puts the sentence in the mouths of the Judaisers precisely so that the council of Acts 15 can strike it down; the verse exists in the New Testament as a claim to be refuted, and its content is a ritual requirement laid on Gentile converts by a party the apostles rule against. Acts 27:31 is Paul on the deck of a foundering ship talking about staying aboard, and is not soteriological at all. A four-word run whose one plausible source is a sentence its own book contradicts is not a borrowing worth cataloguing, though a reader who finds it is owed the account.

“weapons of war” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses and is the King James Bible's ordinary term for military equipment, so no single verse can be named on the phrase alone. The one that tempts is 2 Samuel 1:27, the last line of David's lament over Saul and Jonathan — “How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!” — because Mormon 7 stands immediately after Mormon 6:17-22, this catalogue's most sustained lament over a fallen army, and the transition from lamenting the fallen to naming the weapons of war is the transition David makes. But 2 Samuel 1:27 is an exclamation over weapons destroyed with their owners, and Mormon 7:4 is an imperative to living men to put theirs down; there is no shared verb, no shared syntax, and “weapons of war” is a phrase the Book of Mormon uses dozens of times in the war chapters without any lament attached. The genuine borrowing in this verse is the “delight… in the shedding of blood” construction of Psalm 68:30 plus Hebrews 9:22, linked at the verse.

sharedText: by the ___ of the Father he hath risen again
reason: A near miss worth recording because the miss is in one word and the word is decisive. “glory of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 6:4: “like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.” Mormon 7:5 reads “by the power of the Father he hath risen again”, and “power of the Father” occurs in no KJV verse at all. The setting also invites the identification, since Romans 6:4 grounds the resurrection in baptism and Mormon 7:8 and 7:10 both command baptism. But the substitution of power for glory removes the only rare element the verse had, and the Book of Mormon's construction is a commonplace of its own idiom rather than of the King James Bible's. “risen again” occurs in six KJV verses, none of them attached to the Father. Rejected, and the reader sent to the 1 Corinthians 15:54-57 complex linked at this verse, which accounts for the rest of the sentence.

A four-word run and a genuine machine hit: Revelation 15:2 has “them that had gotten the victory over the beast”, and Mormon 7:5 has “he hath gained the victory over the grave.” The construction is the same and Revelation is the only KJV verse that carries it. It is superseded all the same. “the victory” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, of which 1 Corinthians 15:57 — “thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” — stands four words from “sting of death” and nine from “swallowed up in victory”, both of which Mormon 7:5 also has, and 1 Corinthians 15:55 assigns the victory specifically to the grave, which is Mormon's object. Revelation supplies a preposition; 1 Corinthians supplies the sentence. Adjudicated at this verse as 1 Corinthians 15:55 with 15:54, 15:56 and 15:57 as composite.

“stand before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 14:10, and “judgment seat of Christ” in exactly two, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10; Mormon 7:6's “raised to stand before his judgement seat” has real contact with both. It is not adjudicated here. This catalogue links the Romans / 2 Corinthians composite at Mormon 3:20, earlier in this same book and in the same narrator's voice, where the verse carries the whole fusion — 2 Corinthians's “must”, Romans's “stand”, and 2 Corinthians's tail about receiving according to what is done, whether good or bad — and where mediation-check.py's divergences pointing both ways are set out in full. ADJUDICATING §4 governs: a phrase a narrator has adopted is adjudicated at first use within a book, and 7:6 has only the barest form of it, three words with no distinguishing feature. A reader who arrives at 7:6 should be sent to Mormon 3:20, and to Mormon 6:21 and 3:22 in the same chain. The link written at 7:6 is for a different source, 1 Corinthians 15:54's “brought to pass”.

The highest-scoring candidate the machine offered for this verse, on a five-word run, and it is the wrong sentence entirely. Genesis 16:12 is the angel's oracle about the unborn Ishmael: “he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.” The KJV's idiom there means to live alongside or in defiance of one's kin, not to be admitted to anyone's company, and it is a prophecy of perpetual hostility. Mormon 7:7's clause is a promise of heaven — “to dwell in the presence of God in his kingdom.” Nor is there a better biblical source to substitute: “in the presence of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 1:19 (Gabriel standing there) and Hebrews 9:24 (Christ appearing there for us), and neither uses the verb dwell or refers to the destiny of the redeemed. The clause is the Book of Mormon's own. The adjudicated link at this verse is to the triadic formula at its end.

Acts 10:48 (“commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord”) and Acts 5:40 (“not speak in the name of Jesus”) both scored above Acts 2:38 on the machine's ranking of this verse, on six-word windows. Both are superseded by Acts 2:38, linked here, on a point the windows cannot see: Mormon 7:8 begins “Therefore repent, and be baptized”, and “Repent, and be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:38, which then continues into the same “in the name of Jesus” the other two candidates share. Acts 10:48 reads “of the Lord”, not “of Jesus”, and Acts 5:40 has no baptism in it at all. A standing instance of CONVENTIONS §9: the longest run is not the best source.

One of the register's better entries for this book, because the phrase is rare, the doctrinal setting is adjacent, and the sense is exactly inverted. “first covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 8:7 and Hebrews 9:1, and in both it is a technical term for the Sinai covenant considered as superseded: “if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second”; “then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary”, the sanctuary Hebrews 9:8-9 goes on to call a figure now passing away. Mormon 7:10 uses the phrase for the opposite purpose: “ye are numbered among the people of the first covenant”, offered as a standing reason why the addressees should believe and be baptised. Hebrews' first covenant is the one its readers must be argued out of; Mormon's is the one his readers are to be told they still belong to. Related vocabulary in the same verse points elsewhere and is likewise declined — “seed of Jacob” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Psalm 22:23, Isaiah 45:19, Jeremiah 33:26) and none of them is about a covenanted remnant, and “it shall be well with” occurs in exactly seven and is a KJV commonplace. The verse's adjudicated links are to Matthew 3:11 and to the baptism narrative.
